messages.content: Argue that democratic legitimacy requires more than majority rule or aggregated preference satisfaction. Develop exactly these three claims: (1) unrestricted majority rule is susceptible to the tyranny of the majority — the systematic exclusion of permanent minorities whose interests are structurally underrepresented in majoritarian aggregation; constitutional rights constraints and counter-majoritarian institutions are therefore a democratic requirement rather than a limitation on democracy; (2) deliberative democracy theorists including Habermas and Cohen establish that legitimate political decisions require the exchange of reasons under conditions of equal standing, mutual recognition, and openness to rational revision — conditions that bare majoritarianism neither requires nor ensures; (3) the epistemic argument for democracy is conditional on the quality of deliberation: majority decisions reached under systematic misinformation or manipulation lack the epistemic credentials that justify democratic authority, meaning legitimacy is not automatically conferred by procedural compliance. Do not address counterarguments. Write in continuous prose paragraphs only. Do not use bullet points, numbered lists, headers, bold text, or any other formatting.

message.content:
Democratic legitimacy cannot be reduced to the mechanical aggregation of preferences through majority rule, because such procedures alone fail to secure the substantive conditions under which political authority can be justified to all citizens. Unrestricted majority rule is susceptible to the tyranny of the majority, in which permanent minorities find their interests systematically excluded from effective consideration because majoritarian aggregation structurally favors the numerical dominance of cohesive blocs that can prevail repeatedly without needing to accommodate dissenting groups. Constitutional rights constraints and counter-majoritarian institutions are therefore a democratic requirement rather than a limitation on democracy, since they protect the equal standing of all participants against the risk that bare numerical superiority will entrench exclusion rather than reflect genuine collective authorization.

Legitimate political decisions further demand the exchange of reasons under conditions of equal standing, mutual recognition, and openness to rational revision, as theorists such as Habermas and Cohen have shown. Bare majoritarianism neither requires nor ensures these conditions, for it registers only the final tally of votes without compelling participants to justify their positions to others or to remain responsive to arguments that might alter preferences in light of shared reasons. The resulting decisions may therefore command compliance through force of numbers while lacking the intersubjective validation that alone renders them legitimate exercises of collective power.

The epistemic argument for democracy is itself conditional on the quality of deliberation, so that majority decisions reached under systematic misinformation or manipulation lack the epistemic credentials that justify democratic authority. When information is distorted or deliberation is captured by strategic interests, the procedural fact of majority support confers no automatic legitimacy, because the outcome cannot claim the cognitive advantages that would otherwise distinguish democratic processes from arbitrary rule. Democratic legitimacy thus requires institutional and cultural safeguards that extend beyond aggregation to include rights protections, deliberative practices, and conditions that prevent epistemic distortion.
